title: Wash your feet
hookLine: thirty nuns take Patacara's teaching while washing their feet (Therigatha, the thirty nuns)

cards: Wash your feet, quickly, and sit down to one side. That's the instruction. A group of nuns has come to Patacara, the teacher whose song the path heard yesterday.

The collection calls them the thirty nuns, and they have come for teaching. They might expect a long talk, or some hidden method, or a test. What she gives them starts with water and the dust of the road.

teach.b: First, what she says before the feet. Patacara points at young men pounding grain with pestles. They work hard, and with what they earn they keep a household going, wives and children.
Effort is ordinary, she's saying; people pour it into a home every day. So pour it into the Buddha's teaching, which, she says, no one regrets. Second, the instruction itself.

teach.h: WASH QUICKLY, SIT TO ONE SIDE.
teach.b: Wash your feet quickly, sit to one side, give yourself to calm of mind, and do the teaching. No ceremony. Third, what the nuns do.
The poem repeats her words back as deeds. They washed their feet, sat to one side, gave themselves to calm.
Then the night unfolds, watch by watch. In the first, the poem says, they remembered former lives. In the middle, the divine eye was made clear.
In the last, they tore through the great mass of darkness. Fourth, the morning.

teach.h: BOWING AT HER FEET AT DAWN.
teach.b: They rise, bow at Patacara's feet, and tell her: we have done what you taught. They will honor her, they say, the way the thirty gods honor Indra, unbeaten in battle. Notice the shape of it.
Patacara's own song tells of washing her feet before her night of release. Now she hands that same small gesture to others. The water doesn't wake anyone up, and the poem never says it does.
It's a doorway. You stop walking. You rinse off the road.

how: Some Buddhist monasteries keep water by the door for washing the feet before entering the hall, and some Theravada teachers read the verses of Patacara and her students as a picture of practice that begins in ordinary acts.

o: a bow of greeting to a teacher
the road a nun walks for alms

games.q: Patacara and the nuns: tap the pairs.
p: pound grain to keep a household
the last watch of the night
the mass of darkness torn through

s: in the poem, washing their feet is what frees the nuns
the poem never says that. washing and sitting come first; the night's practice follows.
Patacara's own song also tells of washing her feet
her verses tell of washing her feet before the night she was freed. she passes the same step on.
Patacara gives the nuns a long, secret method
her instruction is short: wash your feet, sit to one side, turn to calm of mind.

games.q: you're one of the nuns who came to Patacara for teaching. she has finished speaking. what do you do?
o: ask her for a longer, deeper teaching.
wash your feet and sit to one side.
go home to think it over.
games.why: the poem repeats her words back as deeds: they washed their feet, sat to one side, and by the last watch of the night had torn through the darkness.

practice: If you can, wash your feet now at a tub or a basin, or your hands if you can't, feeling first the temperature of the water, then the weight under it, and let whatever road you walked today go down the drain.
Patacara said quickly, and quickly here can mean without fuss, not without care. Then sit to one side, dry or damp, and let the breath settle on its own.

wordCard.voice: Pada. The Pali word for foot: Patacara told the nuns to wash their feet, sit to one side, and turn the mind to calm. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali pada: foot. The nuns wash their feet at night, and in the morning bow at Patacara's.

carryVoice: Your line: rinse off the road. The sacred thing and the chore, in one sentence. See you tomorrow.
